problem: Prior VR-demonstration-based personalized navigation (de Heuvel et al. 2022) assumed a static human of known pose and pose-encoded obstacles, so it cannot handle dynamic humans or raw depth-camera input. Learning from high-dimensional depth in dynamic scenes is hard.
motivation: Robots sharing space with people should respect personal preferences (proxemics, trajectory shape, area of navigation), and basic obstacle avoidance cannot do this. Realistic deployment requires a cheap sensor (depth camera) and moving users, which needs a compact state representation for RL.
key_idea: Train a TD3+behavior-cloning navigation policy from VR demonstrations recorded under human motion, using a VAE-compressed depth latent (optionally with an LSTM motion predictor) plus explicit human pose as the state.
insight: Demonstrations drive preference reflection: VAE-ND (plain TD3, no demos) has the worst Fréchet-based preference reflection and shortest-path behavior. The simple VAE-HA outperforms the LSTM human-prediction variant (LSTM-HP) in robustness and preference reflection, so motion prediction did not help. Ablations show a wider 120° FOV does not reduce collisions and removing goal distance does not hurt; the robot still reflects preferences with humans and furniture removed, likely by anchoring on room layout and relative goal.
method: VR demonstration interface (iGibson): user draws a trajectory on the floor with a handheld controller and walks freely while the robot replays it; human pose comes from the HMD; demos are collision-checked and stored in a demo buffer.
TD3 + BC learning: standard TD3 (MLP actor and two critics) with an added behavioral-cloning loss on the actor from a separate demo buffer, balanced by λ_RL=30/4 and λ_BC=10/4; outputs (v, ω).
Sparse reward with demo bias: collision -5, goal +10 (demo) or +5 (training), timeout -2.5, plus a small bonus on demo states to favour demo-like behavior.
β-VAE perception: 128x80 depth image compressed to a 32-D latent (factor 320), trained with 5% dropout noise against noise-free targets.
LSTM predictor: two 64-unit LSTM layers take the last 5 latents, human poses and actions, and predict the next latent and next human pose; the predicted human pose is added to the state (S-LSTM).
Robot-centric state: relative goal (d_G, Δα_G), human presence/pose (d_H, Δα_H; -1 m if not in FOV), and the depth latent.
Deviation-aware Fréchet metric: finds the deviation point t* via a cost cos(φ)f + sin(φ)t with φ=3π/4 and computes the Fréchet distance up to t* to quantify preference reflection.

setting.backbone: TD3 MLP actor/critics with β-VAE (+ LSTM predictor in one variant), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Around 9 scene configurations with ~3 self-recorded VR demonstration trajectories each; RL in iGibson scenes with randomized human behaviors; VAE/LSTM trained on an extensive self-generated iGibson depth dataset
setting.observation: Forward depth camera (87° HFOV, 6 m range, 128x80) plus human pose when in FOV and relative goal position
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (v in [0,0.5] m/s, ω in [-π,π] rad/s)
setting.privileged: Human pose/presence in FOV (ground-truth from simulator) and relative goal position are given to the policy; VAE/LSTM trained with GT human data

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (trajectory plots, success/collision/timeout bar chart, Fréchet plots); no numeric tables and no standard benchmark.
results: VAE-HA yields the most robust and best preference-reflecting behavior, with the smallest deviation-aware Fréchet distance; no-demo TD3 (VAE-ND) and LSTM-HP are worse. Demonstration-aware VAE variants have the fewest collisions, and mode-5 (demo) human behavior gives the best success. Only qualitative/figure-based results are reported.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation with demonstrations recorded by the authors (few demos, no new user study), and the policy is given ground-truth human detection/pose.
The predictor gave no benefit, and collisions remain more frequent than timeouts.
Single forward camera, no backward driving, single human only.
builds_on: de Heuvel et al. 2022 (VR + RL personalized navigation)
